newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Street battles rage in conquered Afghan town.
newsitem.headline: Street battles rage in conquered Afghan town.

text.p: The Taleban Islamic militia fought fierce street battles with Shi'ite Moslems through the night and into Wednesday in this newly conquered northern Afghan town, witnesses said.
Rival factions traded small arms and machine gun fire and explosions from heavier weapons shook Mazar-i-Sharif.
The fighting erupted on Tuesday afternoon when the purist Taleban sent a column of tanks and armoured personnel carriers into the northern Saidabad district, inhabited by Shi'ite Moslem Hazaras.

Witnesses said armed Shi'ites fought the Taleban forces who were being attacked in the rear by their ostensible allies, ethnic Uzbek troops which captured Mazar-i-Sharif from opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum on Saturday.
The clashes spread across wide areas of Mazar-i-Sharif as the Taleban, which are thought to have at least 3,000 fighters in the city, sought to reinforce their units in Saidabad.
Ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Malik allied with the Taleban last week after staging a mutiny against Dostum.
Malik's men, who had forced Dostum to flee Afghanistan on Saturday, were supposed to be operating jointly with the Taleban in the north.
The Taleban had moved into the mainly Hazara tribe district of Mazar-i-Sharif to disarm local people seen as supporters of the anti-Taleban Hezb-i-Wahadat militia force.
Separately, other Taleban forces have reported crossing a key pass into opposition areas.

The Taleban government said its forces had crossed the strategic Salang Pass north of the capital Kabul and marched deep into former opposition territory after being blocked by shelling and a damaged road.

The United Arab Emirates on Tuesday became the third nation to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government, which was was set up after the militia, led by Islamic theology students, captured Kabul last September and which controls nearly 90 percent of the war-shattered country.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have already recognised the Taleban government.
The United States called on Tuesday for an end to fighting in Afghanistan but left unclear whether it would accord diplomatic recognition.

The State Department urged the creation of a "broadly representative government" in Afghanistan and told the Taleban they would need to moderate their policies if they hoped to attract Western aid to rebuild the war-shattered country.
"The United States continues to urge an immediate end to fighting," spokesman John Dinger said.
Dinger dodged questions on whether the United States planned to accept the Taleban as the government of Afghanistan, saying that Washington "recognizes states, not governments."
Despite maintaining contacts with the Taleban, Washington has avoided getting too close to the movement, partly due to hostile U.S. media coverage of the militia's tough restrictions on women.
